title: Compare building a modern React CRUD application with REST versus GraphQL. Understand query shapes, state mutations, and implementation patterns
summary: This article compares building the same React CRUD feature using REST versus GraphQL approaches against a unified backend, demonstrating how REST requires sequential/parallel requests while GraphQL enables single queries. It addresses a common architecture debate with practical, runnable code examples rather than theory.
content:
Whenever I start a new client project or evaluate an architecture for a team, I inevitably get asked the same question:
"Should we build our frontend using REST or GraphQL?"
A few months ago, I was architecting a dashboard feature that needed to display user profiles, their published articles, and nested comment threads.
The REST advocates pushed for standard endpoints (/users, /posts, /comments), while frontend engineers worried about waterfall network requests (GET /users/1, then GET /users/1/posts, then GET /posts/:id/comments). The GraphQL advocates wanted a single query, while the backend team worried about schema complexity.
When I wanted to build a quick side-by-side prototype to settle the debate with real code, I ran into an absurd roadblock: I couldn't find a single mock backend that supported both REST and GraphQL queries on the exact same underlying dataset with mutation support.
I had to either spend an entire weekend building two separate mock servers, or give up on an authentic side-by-side comparison.
That frustration was a huge driver behind adding a native GraphQL gateway to Playground API — allowing developers to query the exact same data via REST or GraphQL side-by-side with zero setup.
In this post, we're skipping the theoretical internet debates. I'll show you how to build the exact same React CRUD feature using both approaches against a unified, live backend sandbox.
Let's build a user profile screen that needs to display:
User details (name, email, company)
The user's published blog posts
The latest comments on each post
Let's look at how REST and GraphQL approach this data requirement.
In standard REST architecture, resources are organized around distinct URL endpoints.
To get the user and their related posts and comments, a REST client typically executes sequential or parallel HTTP GET requests:
1. GET /api/v1/users/1           ──► Fetches User profile
2. GET /api/v1/users/1/posts     ──► Fetches User's posts
3. GET /api/v1/posts/10/comment

title: NFT 재평가: 투기 광풍 너머의 기술적 토대를 짚어보다
summary: Dismissing NFTs as failed technology oversimplifies their underlying innovation in verifiable digital scarcity and programmable assets, according to this analysis tracing NFT history from Colored Coins through ERC-721. The article argues that core technological principles remain viable despite the 2021-2022 market collapse driven by speculation rather than technical flaws.
content: NFT, 즉 대체 불가능 토큰이라는 용어는 2021년 주류 의식 속에 폭발적으로 등장하며, 모호했던 블록체인 기술을 문화적, 금융적 현상으로 탈바꿈시켰다. 만화 원숭이 디지털 이미지는 수백만 달러에 팔렸고, 가상 토지는 터무니없는 가격에 거래되었으며, 미술계는 소유권의 새로운 패러다임과 씨름해야 했다. 그러나 급부상했던 만큼이나 빠르게, NFT 시장은 2022년 말부터 극적인 침체기를 겪으며 광범위한 회의론과 함께 NFT가 단지 투기적 거품, 한때의 유행, 심지어는 근본적으로 실패한 기술이라는 인식이 팽배해졌다. 이 글은 이러한 인식을 비판적으로 분석하며, 대체 불가능 토큰의 근본적인 기술과 초기 급등을 특징지었던 투기적 시장 행태를 구분하고자 한다. NFT를 "실패한 기술"로 단정하는 것은 그 이면에 깔린 혁신과 장기적인 잠재력을 무시하는 지나친 단순화일 수밖에 없다. 초기 애플리케이션, 특히 디지털 수집품과 투기적 미술 분야에서 지속 불가능한 평가와 그에 따른 붕괴를 겪었지만, NFT의 핵심 기술 원칙인 검증 가능한 디지털 희소성, 불변의 소유권 기록, 그리고 프로그래밍 가능한 디지털 자산은 여전히 견고하며 지속적으로 진화하고 있다. 이번 분석에서는 NFT의 기술적 기반을 깊이 파고들고, 헤드라인을 장식했던 이슈 너머의 실제 적용 사례들을 검토하며, 내재된 한계점들을 탐구한다. 궁극적으로는 이 기술이 시장 변동성에도 불구하고 실패작인지, 아니면 아직 개발 및 채택 초기 단계에 있는 강력한 신생 혁신인지에 대한 전문가적 관점을 제시할 것이다. NFT의 "실패"를 둘러싼 논쟁을 이해하려면, 먼저 그 근본적인 성격과 역사적 궤적을 파악하는 것이 필수적이다. NFT는 블록체인에 기록된 고유한 디지털 식별자로, 디지털 자산 또는 물리적 자산의 토큰화된 버전에 대한 소유권과 진위 여부를 증명하는 데 사용된다. 비트코인이나 이더리움처럼 각 단위가 서로 교환 가능한 대체 가능한(fungible) 암호화폐와 달리, NFT는 대체 불가능하다는 점에서 고유하며 다른 동일한 항목으로 대체될 수 없다. 이러한 고유성은 블록체인의 암호화 특성에 의해 보장되며, 소유권에 대한 불변하고 공개적으로 검증 가능한 기록을 제공한다. 대체 불가능 토큰의 기원은 2012년 비트코인 네트워크에서 특정 속성으로 표시되어 다른 자산을 나타낼 수 있었던 Colored Coins와 같은 초기 블록체인 실험으로 거슬러 올라간다. 이후 2014년 Counterparty 플랫폼은 사용자 생성 디지털 자산 생성을 용이하게 했다. 그러나 NFT의 현대 시대는 2017년 이더리움 블록체인에 ERC-721 표준이 도입되면서 진정으로 시작되었다. 이 표준은 고유한 대체 불가능 디지털 자산을 생성하기 위한 견고하고 널리 채택된 프레임워크를 제공했다. 블록체인 기반 게임으로 사용자들이 고유한 디지털 고양이를 수집하고 번식시킬 수 있었던 CryptoKitties의 출시는 ERC-721의 잠재력과 한계를 명확히 보여주며, 전례 없는 인기로 인해 이더리움 네트워크에 상당한 혼잡을 야기하기도 했다. 이후 몇 년 동안 NFT 채택은 점진적으로 증가했고, 2021년과 2022년 초에 폭발적인 성장을 정점에 달했다. 이 시기는 전례 없는 거래량, 유명인 지지, 그리고 디지털 아트 및 수집품의 기록적인 판매로 특징지어진다. 그러나 2022년 중반에 접어들면서 금리 인상, 광범위한 암호화폐 시장 침체, 투기적 열기 냉각 등 여러 요인이 복합적으로 작용하여 NFT 가격과 거래 활동이 급격히 감소했다. 이러한 시장 조정은 NFT가 과대평가된 거품에 불과하다는 인식을 부채질했고, 핵심적인 질문을 던지게 했다. 기술 자체에 결함이 있는 것일까, 아니면 단순히 시장의 비이성적인 과열이 꺾인 것일까? NFT 개념의 핵심은 검증 가능한 디지털 희소성과 소유권을 가능하게 하기 위해 여러 강력한 블록체인 기술을 활용한다. 이러한 기술적 기반을 이해하는 것은 기술 자체가 "실패"인지 여부를 평가하는 데 결정적인 역할을 한다. NFT는 근본적으로 블록체인 원장의 불변성에 의존한다. NFT가 발행될 때, 고유

title: AI Agent for Home Services: Lead Intake That Prices Jobs
summary: Home services AI agents must handle three unique requirements: distinguishing emergencies, capturing job details for pricing, and respecting geography—areas where generic chatbots fail and create liability. The article details what information agents need, pre-approved safety responses, and proper escalation rules to balance automation with accountability.
content:
Home services break normal chatbot designs: emergencies can't wait, jobs can't be priced blind, and geography matters. Here is the triage, intake and dispatch setup that works.
I audited a two-van plumbing firm's phone log last autumn. In one week: 34 missed calls, 29 of them landing on voicemail, and 11 that were clearly new jobs. Every one of those 11 went to whichever competitor answered next — and at least three were emergencies the firm could have charged its call-out fee for.
Home services is the industry where after-hours coverage pays for itself fastest, and also the one where a generic chatbot design fails hardest. The failure isn't technology. It's that home-services conversations have three properties most deployments never plan for: some messages are emergencies with safety implications, most jobs cannot be priced from a chat, and geography decides whether the lead is worth anything at all. Get all three right and the agent becomes the best employee the firm has. Miss one and it creates liability at 2am.
The first job of a home-services agent is not answering questions. It is deciding, fast, whether the message is an emergency. That means the emergency list must be written down, agreed with the owner, and phrased as a list — not a paragraph. For plumbing, the list is short: gas smell, burst pipe or active flooding, sewage backup, no water at all, and water near electrics.
What the agent is allowed to say about an emergency is equally narrow:
Safety lines the owner has pre-approved, word for word — for example, where the main water shutoff usually is and to close it. Nothing beyond the approved lines, ever.
The emergency call-out fee and how dispatch works, quoted from the facts file.
Confirmation that the on-call van is being paged, with the address and callback number it captured.
What it may never say: "that sounds fine until morning," any diagnosis of the cause, or any assessment of danger. An agent that reassures a caller about a gas smell is a liabi

title: AI Chatbot Order Status: Cutting WISMO for Small Shops
summary: "Where is my order" queries consume half of small shop support tickets but are safely automatable by AI agents that read order data accurately and verify customer identity. The article defines strict data access rules, dangerous information agents must never touch, and how proper design prevents liability while cutting repetitive work.
content:
"Where is my order" is the highest-volume, lowest-risk question a small shop gets. Here is what a WISMO agent needs, the three answers that cover most of it, and when to escalate.
A nine-person store selling kitchenware pulled its support inbox for me last month: 640 tickets over four weeks, and by my count 390 of them were some version of "where is my order." Two people spent most of every working day answering them by opening the order system, opening the carrier's site, and copying the same three facts back to the customer.
That ratio is not unusual. In the small shops I've worked with, WISMO — where is my order — plus its cousins "where is my refund" and "has it shipped" routinely makes up half or more of inbound tickets. It is also the safest high-volume query to automate, for one structural reason: the answer already exists in a system. There is no judgement in "shipped Tuesday, tracking link here, latest scan is Memphis." An agent that reads that data back accurately is indistinguishable from a person who does, except faster and at 3am.
But the same structural property cuts the other way: an agent that guesses at order data produces confident nonsense, and a customer holding a tracking number will find out. So the whole design hangs on what the agent can see, what it may say, and where it stops.
Keep the read scope deliberately small. For each order, the agent needs:
Order number, status (received, processing, shipped, delivered), and the date of each state change
Ship date, carrier, and tracking number
The latest carrier scan event, verbatim
The promised dispatch window and the backorder date if flagged
And it needs one lookup rule: an order is only revealed when both the order number and the email on the order match. Order numbers get forwarded, screenshotted and half-remembered; matching on the number alone hands a stranger's order details to whoever types it in.
What it must never see or touch:
Full card data. A properly run store doesn't hold it anyway —

title: Before you blame EF Core for a slow API, check this.
summary: Common API slowness causes lie beyond database queries: thread pool starvation from blocking async calls, connection pool exhaustion, transaction locking, JSON serialization overhead, and hidden middleware work. The article helps developers diagnose actual bottlenecks before blaming ORM frameworks.
content:
"The query is slow" is one of the most common misdiagnoses I see. Often, the query is fine, and the problem lies elsewhere. Next time you hit a slow endpoint, check these too.
⚡𝗧𝗵𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗱 𝗽𝗼𝗼𝗹 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗿𝘃𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻
You call DoSomethingAsync() and then block on it with .Wait() or .Result. That thread now sits there waiting, and another thread from the pool may be needed to finish the async work.
Under a burst of requests, this quickly eats up thread pool threads, and the whole API slows down, not just that endpoint.
⚡𝗖𝗼𝗻𝗻𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗽𝗼𝗼𝗹 𝗲𝘅𝗵𝗮𝘂𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻
Quite similar to thread pool starvation, but for database connections. Once the app has used up every available connection, new requests have to wait for one to free up. The query itself might take 5ms, but the request waits seconds before it even runs.
Common causes: connections or DbContexts not disposed properly, long-running queries, or a pool size that's too small for your load.
⚡𝗟𝗼𝗰𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗯𝗹𝗼𝗰𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗴
Locking is normal. SQL Server locks data while a transaction works with it, so another transaction can't make a conflicting change at the same time.
Blocking is when another transaction has to wait for that lock. A little is fine. It becomes a problem when a transaction holds the lock for too long, and your "slow" query is really just stuck in a queue.
⚡𝗦𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗮𝗹𝗶𝘇𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻
Turning a large or deeply nested object into JSON takes time. Returning entities directly is a common trap because navigation properties can pull in huge object graphs. Return DTOs with only what the client needs.
⚡𝗛𝗶𝗱𝗱𝗲𝗻 𝗽𝗲𝗿-𝗿𝗲𝗾𝘂𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸
Before a request reaches your controller, it may already go through logging, tracing, auth checks, and other middleware. After the controller, there's serialization, response logging, and so on.
Most of this is necessary. But an expensive logging setup or one extra DB call in an auth handler runs on every single request. Know what happens before and a

title: Choose first-match or all-matches routing before attaching any sender
summary: The us-brand-signal-rule-router Actor defines routing contracts (first-match vs all-matches mode) for signals before connecting external notification senders, allowing rules to be inspected and tested as data labels. This approach resolves overlapping rules and unmatched records before triggering any actual external actions.
content:
Suppose one signal matches both an urgent-review rule and a broad catch-all rule. Should it receive one route or both? That question belongs in the routing contract before anyone attaches a notification sender. An inspectable route plan lets you resolve rule order, overlaps, and unmatched records while the outcome is still a set of labels rather than an external action.
I maintain the us-brand-signal-rule-router Actor. This walkthrough describes its published build 0.2.2, inspected on 16 October 2026. The example below is synthetic and reviewed against that contract; it was not executed for this article. AI-assisted drafting was followed by a separate factual and editorial review.
The Rule Router takes supplied signals, ordered rules, and a mode. firstMatch chooses the first matching rule; allMatches retains matches in rule order. Match bounds are inclusive and null fields are wildcards. The example uses one complete signal and one wildcard rule. All nullable match fields still need to be present. Its observation timestamp includes UTC milliseconds, as this contract requires.
{
  "schemaVersion": "1.1",
  "mode": "firstMatch",
  "signals": [
    {
      "signalId": "sig-1",
      "brandName": "Example Brand",
      "eventType": "other",
      "severity": "low",
      "confidence": 0.5,
      "sourceName": "Synthetic note",
      "country": "US",
      "analysisStatus": "unreviewed",
      "observedAt": "2026-10-01T08:00:00.000Z"
    }
  ],
  "rules": [
    {
      "ruleId": "rule-1",
      "routeId": "review-1",
      "eventType": null,
      "severity": null,
      "confidenceMin": null,
      "confidenceMax": null,
      "sourceName": null,
      "country": null,
      "analysisStatus": null
    }
  ]
}

title: Website Error Logs: A Practical Way to Investigate Without Exposing Secrets
summary: Practical guidance for collecting and analyzing error logs to diagnose failures while protecting sensitive data like tokens and passwords, with techniques for tracing requests through multiple system layers. The article covers forming diagnostic hypotheses and safely sharing findings without exposing confidential information.
content:
An error page tells you that something failed. Logs can help explain why, but only when they are collected with enough context and handled responsibly.
Note the affected URL, approximate time, action taken, and response status. Include the timezone. A request identifier is useful when the application provides one.
Avoid immediately changing several settings. Preserve the relevant evidence so later observations can be compared with the original failure.
A reverse proxy, web server, application runtime, and database may each record a different part of the same request. Start at the public symptom and follow the request through the relevant layers.
An HTTP 500 status alone does not identify a database failure. Read the associated error and investigate the dependency it actually names.
Do not publish raw logs in a forum without review. Remove access tokens, cookies, passwords, personal information, and confidential query data. Keep the surrounding error context needed for diagnosis.
In production, avoid displaying detailed stack traces to visitors. Use controlled logging and restricted access instead.
Form a hypothesis, apply a targeted correction, and repeat the failing action. Confirm both the visible behavior and the relevant log output.
Document what changed and how it can be reversed. If the cause remains unclear, share a sanitized excerpt and the reproduction steps with the responsible support team.
Set retention and rotation appropriate to the service. Logs that fill the disk can become an availability problem themselves.
Published for Alif Host. Good troubleshooting improves observability without making private data public.
A visitor can load a contact page but receives an error after submitting it. The initial page request and the form submission are separate operations. Checking only the page response will miss the failing action.

title: Where to publish your browser game in 2026
summary: Guidance for publishing browser games prioritizes first impressions—fast loading, mobile compatibility, and good link previews—over discovery mechanics, followed by hosting options including GitHub Pages, Netlify, Vercel, and itch.io. The checklist approach emphasizes that retention and sharing depend on initial user experience.
content:
I'm Kyle, and I run Foundplay, a free discovery platform for browser games, so I have a stake in one of the options below. I've tried to describe every site from its own pages, linked them, and kept Foundplay to one section. The checklist part is useful wherever you post.
You finished a game that runs in a browser. Here's how to get it in front of people, in the order I'd do it.
A listing sends people to your game once. These three things decide whether they stay and share it.
It loads fast. Show a title screen or loading bar within a few seconds. Compress images and audio, and load big assets after the first screen. Throttle the network in your browser's dev tools and watch what a player on a slow connection sees.
It works on a phone, or says it doesn't. A lot of links get opened on phones. Pointer events give you mouse, touch and pen with one set of handlers. Add a viewport meta tag and stop the page scrolling during play. If the game really needs a keyboard, say so on the first screen.
Links to it preview well. Without Open Graph tags, a shared link is a bare URL in Discord or a group chat:
<title>Your Game: a one line pitch</title>
<meta name="description" content="What the player does, in one sentence.">
<meta property="og:title" content="Your Game">
<meta property="og:description" content="What the player does, in one sentence.">
<meta property="og:image" content="https://example.com/share.png">
<meta name="twitter:card" content="summary_large_image">

The image needs an absolute URL, about 1200 by 630 pixels.
Free options for a public link:
GitHub Pages: free for public repositories (docs).
Netlify: a free plan. Netlify Drop publishes a folder or zip you drag in.
Vercel: a free Hobby plan, but its docs limit Hobby to non-commercial, personal use. If the game shows ads or sells anything, use another host.
itch.io: upload a zip with an index.html, or a single HTML file, and it plays on your page (HTML5 docs).

title: Windows 11 Snap Shortcuts: Arrange Windows With Win + Arrow Keys
summary: Windows 11 keyboard shortcuts (Win+Left/Right for half-screen, Win+Up/Down for quarters and maximize) enable efficient side-by-side workflows without manual window dragging. Common use cases include comparing documents, copying data between applications, and keeping meeting windows visible while working.
content:
Working with a report on one side and source material on the other is a common setup. Getting there by dragging window edges with the mouse rarely lines up exactly, and you redo it each time a window gets moved.
TL;DR: Win+Left or Win+Right snaps a window to half the screen; Win+Up and Win+Down resize it.
Win+Left / Win+Right snaps the active window to the left or right half of the screen. Report on the left, reference on the right.
Win+Up makes the window bigger. On a window that's snapped to one half, the first press moves it to the top quarter of the screen; press it again to fill the screen.
Win+Down restores a maximized window to its previous size.
All of these were pressed and checked on Windows 11.
After Win+Right, Windows shows a list of your other open windows on the empty left side. Click one and it fills the left half immediately. This is Snap Assist, and it means you only need one shortcut to set up a side-by-side view.
Comparing two documents, copying numbers from a PDF into a spreadsheet, reading a ticket while writing code, or keeping a meeting window open next to your notes. Any task where your eyes go back and forth between two windows gets easier when both are fully visible.
On a wide monitor, quarters are useful too: a half-screen window plus two quarter windows lets you keep three things in view without overlap.
The shortcut acts on the active window. If the wrong window moves, click the one you meant first, then press the keys.
Win+Up on a half-snapped window doesn't maximize right away; it goes to a quarter first. People often assume it didn't work and give up after one press.
If Snap Assist doesn't appear, snapping options may be turned off in Settings under multitasking.
If the half and quarter layouts aren't enough, Microsoft's free PowerToys includes FancyZones, which lets you define your own layout grid. For most two-window work, the built-in shortcuts above cover it without installing anything.

title: Your AI quoted $1,850. Your salesperson quoted $2,400. The customer saw both.
summary: A commercial cleaning company's AI agent quoted incorrect prices because it read from a 2023 price sheet while salespeople used 2025 data and the CRM had a third set—demonstrating a data governance problem, not hallucination. The article prescribes nominating a single authoritative price source with version control instead of tuning prompts.
content:
A commercial cleaning company asked me to look at their AI receptionist because "it keeps giving the wrong prices." I pulled 143 quotes from one quarter — every enquiry where the AI had produced a number and a human had later quoted the same job.
59 of them disagreed. That's 41%. The average gap was 18%, and in one case the AI said $1,850 and the account manager quoted $2,400 for the same square footage and the same frequency.
The customer had both numbers in writing, four days apart.
My first assumption was hallucination. It wasn't. I read the transcripts. The AI was reading from a real document — a 2023 price sheet in a shared drive. The salesperson was reading from a 2025 sheet in his own email. The CRM had a third set of numbers that matched neither.
Three sources of truth, all of them officially correct, none of them reconciled:



Source
Who used it
Last updated
Monthly minimum




Price sheet v3 (shared drive)
AI agent
March 2023
$480


Price sheet v5 (sales inbox)
Account managers
Jan 2025
$620


CRM product list
Quotes generated in CRM
Partial migration
$550



The AI wasn't wrong. It was consistently loyal to a document nobody had retired. That's a much easier problem to fix, and a much worse one to leave alone — because a customer who catches you quoting two prices doesn't conclude "their data is messy." They conclude "they're making it up as they go."
Quote consistency is a data governance problem wearing a prompt's clothing. If you tune the prompt first, you will make the agent more confident about the wrong number.
The fix starts before any prompt work. Nominate exactly one artefact as the price authority and give it a version and an expiry date. Everything else becomes a derived copy that is allowed to be wrong, because it's not the authority.
Here's the structure I use. One file, one row per sellable unit, no prose:
sku,unit,list_price,min_qty,tier_2_qty,tier_2_price,floor_price,effective_from,expires,notes
CLEAN-STD-SQFT,sqft,0.14,2000,5000,0.11,0.0

title: Designing approvals
summary: Risk-based approval workflows approve read operations automatically, log routine updates, and require human review only for consequential actions—reversing org-chart-driven approval that stalls low-risk work. The article emphasizes that approval rules often exist unwritten in practice and must be codified so agents can enforce them.
content:
Not every action deserves the same approval. A read-only lookup risks nothing. A routine update risks a little. A consequential action risks a lot.
Most approval flows ignore that. They follow the org chart instead of the risk. Everything waits for the same manager. Everything takes the same two days. The low-risk work stalls, and the high-risk work gets the same rubber stamp as everything else.
Practitioners wrote the real rules for us, and none of them are in any API contract. Testimonials need a human before they go live. Escalation happens after two contacts. Refunds under fifty dollars are fine when the order is paid and never refunded before. Timeline rules nobody wrote down anywhere.
Those are not edge cases. Those are the approval flow. The risk lives in the unwritten rule, not in the endpoint. An agent that cannot see the rule cannot follow it, no matter how clean the permission model looks.
Design approvals around the risk. Let the read go through. Let the routine update go through with a log. Make the consequential action wait for a named human, with the reason attached.
What is the highest-risk action your agent can take today without asking anyone.

title: Claude Code Agent Loop Deep Dive (7): Retries and Eight Layers of Error Recovery
summary: Claude Code's withRetry mechanism handles infrastructure failures through layered strategies including configurable retry counts, server-directed backoff, and error classification that distinguishes retryable from non-retryable failures. The approach respects server headers that indicate retry eligibility while maintaining a single-request interface to the outer loop.
content:
Earlier posts covered semantic recovery inside the agent loop: raising the output-token limit, compacting an overlong context, and handling stop reasons. A production agent also encounters infrastructure failures:
The network fails before a request reaches the API.
The API returns a 500 server error.
A 429 rate limit is reached.
A 529 reports an overloaded Anthropic cluster.
The API rejects the request as prompt_too_long.
Claude Code does not handle those cases with one generic retry. It layers retries, server-directed backoff, model fallback, context recovery, and hard stop conditions so that a single user request has the best possible chance of finishing without manual intervention.
withRetry


Claude Code never makes a bare model request. Every logical call_llm is wrapped by withRetry, so one apparent call may be one to ten actual HTTP requests.
Its core behavior is:
DEFAULT_MAX_RETRIES = 10.
CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_RETRIES can override that default.
On failure, decide whether the error is retryable.
If retryable, wait according to the backoff policy and send the request again.
If not retryable, return the failure to the outer loop immediately.
The main loop therefore sees an API call as either a final success or a final failure. The transient request attempts remain hidden inside withRetry.
The naïve approach is to classify errors entirely in the client: retry 500 and 429, never retry 400.
Claude Code instead asks the server first. Anthropic error responses can include:
x-should-retry: true

or:
x-should-retry: false

If that header is present, it takes precedence over the HTTP status. The client uses its own status-code, error-type, and response-body heuristics only when the header is absent—for example, an overloaded_error in the body can still be recognized as retryable.
This is a production-friendly pattern. The service knows more about its current cluster state and can change retry semantics without requiring every client to ship an update. Client heuristics remain
